query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting a small fraction (≈2 atomic %) of Zr for W in equiatomic NbMoTaW will increase room-temperature tensile ductility (>3 % uniform elongation versus ≤1 % for the baseline) while retaining (±5 %) the 1600 °C yield strength and showing no more than ±20 % change in irradiation-induced hardening after 3 MeV Fe ion doses up to 5 dpa, because oversized Zr atoms (a) segregate to grain boundaries to improve cohesion and (b) locally lower the Peierls barrier in the BCC lattice, promoting <111> dislocation glide without degrading the solid-solution-strengthened matrix that controls high-temperature strength and point-defect recombination.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, homogenized, single-phase BCC equiatomic NbMoTaW alloy (grain size 20–50 µm).
generation.intervention: Add 2 at.% Zr at the expense of W, producing (Nb0.25Mo0.25Ta0.25W0.23Zr0.02) alloy; fabricate by arc melting, homogenize at 1200 °C/24 h, water quench.
generation.conditions: Evaluate (i) tensile tests at 25 °C (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹); (ii) compression or tensile tests at 1600 °C in vacuum (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹); (iii) 3 MeV Fe²⁺ ion irradiation at 600 °C to 5 dpa followed by room-temperature nano-indentation.
generation.structural_mediator: Zr-rich atomic-scale segregation layers (≤1 nm) at grain boundaries plus locally distorted BCC lattice around Zr oversized solutes.
generation.mechanism: 1. Grain-boundary cohesion: Zr segregation lowers local grain-boundary energy, reducing premature intergranular fracture that dominates the brittle response of baseline NbMoTaW at 25 °C. 2. Dislocation mobility: Zr’s lower shear modulus and large atomic size create local soft zones that decrease the Peierls barrier for screw dislocation motion, allowing dislocation multiplication at low temperatures and increasing ductility. 3. High-temperature strength retained because the overall solid-solution strengthening from Nb–Mo–Ta–W matrix is only slightly reduced (Δσy <5 %) for a 2 % substitution, and Zr’s high melting point (~1855 °C) maintains lattice stability. 4. Irradiation resistance maintained or slightly improved as oversized Zr atoms act as efficient sinks for self-interstitials and vacancies, enhancing recombination and limiting defect cluster growth.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to baseline NbMoTaW: • 25 °C: uniform elongation rises from ≤1 % to >3 %; yield strength decreases ≤10 %. • 1600 °C: 0.2 % yield stress and creep rate change ≤5 %. • Irradiated state (5 dpa, 600 °C): nano-indentation hardness change ≤±20 % of baseline; dislocation loop density comparable or reduced.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic NbMoTaW (no Zr) tested under identical thermal-mechanical and irradiation conditions.
generation.boundary: Valid for Zr additions in the dilute regime (0.5–3 at. %) and for single-phase BCC microstructures with grain sizes 10–100 µm; larger Zr contents or presence of Laves/hexagonal precipitates fall outside scope.
generation.uncertainty: Moderate: Zr may form Laves-phase precipitates if segregation is uncontrolled; actual ductility gain depends on grain-boundary chemistry distribution, which is processing-sensitive.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three 20 g alloy buttons: (1) baseline NbMoTaW, (2) NbMoTaW+2 at.% Zr, (3) NbMoTaW+4 at.% Zr (out-of-bounds check). Homogenize identically. Perform: a) room-temperature tensile tests, n=5 per alloy; b) 1600 °C compression tests; c) irradiate polished samples with 3 MeV Fe²⁺ ions at 600 °C to 5 dpa, then nano-indent and TEM characterise.
measurements: Uniform elongation and yield strength at 25 °C
Yield strength or 0.2 % proof stress at 1600 °C
Nano-indentation hardness change pre- and post-irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Hypothesis is falsified if any of the following occur for the 2 at.% Zr alloy: (i) uniform elongation ≤1 % or not statistically higher (p>0.05) than baseline; (ii) 1600 °C yield strength decreases by >10 % or creep rate increases >10 %; (iii) irradiation-induced hardness increase exceeds baseline by >20 % or defect density doubles.
